utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We reassemble as contingently foreshadowed yesterday for the purpose of rebuttal evidence. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good morning. The preliminary inquiry, confirmation that I wanted to ask of the Chamber is that -- our understanding that the rebuttal is permitted in two areas; namely, the alleged briefing on the 5th of December in Kupari and the alleged telephone conversation with General Kadijevic on 6th of December. We realise we have a very limited time, and we have prepared accordingly. We wish to clarify that the cross-examination will be strictly limited to those two areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any submission, Mr. Rodic or Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, as for the cross-examination of Admiral Jokic, it goes without saying that it will be in relation to these two subject matters. However, I would like to ask for the Chamber's understanding. It must be understood that these limitations cannot be so strict as to avoid mentioning anything that might be indirectly related to the rebuttal in this case. The focus will be on the subject matters directly related to the rebuttal. However, there is other related information, what went before the event itself and what came after. Both these are subject matters of the rebuttal and are directly related to the event under consideration. We will move within that framework, but we would like to point out that there is a history to these events, what immediately preceded the event and also there were consequences over the following days after that event. That is the first thing we wish to point out, Your Honour. And the second thing we wanted to bring up is the following: During the Defence case, whenever a document surfaced with the 9th VPS in the header, our learned friend and colleagues raised objections. That was sometimes admitted by the Trial Chamber and were sometimes overruled. I'm saying in relation to documents related to the 9th VPS. There are three specific documents that the Defence obtained following Admiral Jokic's testimony that in terms of their substance could not be placed before the Trial Chamber through any other witness, precisely because of their substance. And these were drafted and signed or written and signed by Admiral Jokic personally. In view of the standing objection to the effect that that has to do with Admiral Jokic must be shown or put to Admiral Jokic, and in order to have a fair trial, in short, for General Strugar as we believe these elements to be relevant for this case and for the Chamber's decision, may we please be granted leave to put these two or three documents to Admiral Jokic so that he could respond. In addition to that, there's another document that was forwarded to OTP by the Defence team seven days ago, another document which is relevant to Admiral Jokic's testimony and which was submitted to the Defence team without any translation as late as seven days ago. We would like to ask permission to put to Admiral Jokic a small portion of that document as well. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, this document provided some seven days ago, do you have a position in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure which document is referred to. If anything were provided, it would have been pursuant to an ongoing Rule 68 obligation. And I do not know which document would be provided. We would ask, of course, to have a look at it, and if need be to have a moment with the admiral on any documents that might be asked of him. I do not know -- again, I'm in the dark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, can you identify the document for Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I can, Your Honour. I am talking about the document that the OTP submitted on the 15th of July in connection with Zeljko Soldo. I'm not sure how those documents were obtained or what they have to do with Zeljko Soldo because that was not disclosed. Nevertheless, I'm speaking about those documents. And one of the documents is the diary which speaks about the alleged visit to Zarkovica by Lieutenant General Zivota Panic, General Strugar, and Admiral Jokic. The Chamber will surely remember that Admiral Jokic spoke about that, claiming that this visit happened on the 14th of December 1991. However, if we look at the document that was provided by the OTP, it is clear that the visit under discussion is the one that happened three months later, on the -- more than three months later, on the 25th of March 1992. So that would be the substance of the document I am speaking about. It was disclosed to us on the 15th of July this year. It wasn't made clear whether that was a Rule 68 disclosure or perhaps pursuant to another rule. But that is what we got from our learned friends and colleagues from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may clarify, Your Honour, if a document comes into the possession of the OTP and it is not clear whether it is 68 or not, but there is a possibility, we err on the side the caution, and I believe the explanation was it had just been received and it was transmitted almost immediately. In terms of having a look at the document, we'll have to recall it and find the document ourselves. And if we need -- well, it would be very difficult, I believe, once the witness is actually sworn, to have any discussions. So in principle, issues concerning questioning, we would have preferred that it be raised earlier. I think it would be very difficult to meet now on that. I would ask the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, if this is a document which has just been discovered for the first time in the last week to the Defence on an issue which was the subject of testimony --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- not only from the admiral but others, there would seem to be some justification for it being able to be raised at this time. Are you saying that you need five minutes to discuss it with the admiral before his evidence commences? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it's possible, that document and any other documents that the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm talking only about the one document, which is the diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, we would certainly ask to have an opportunity. And Your Honour, if I may ask, inquire, on any other documents that -- where a 90(H) aspect is raised, if there is inquiry, then those will not have been put to the admiral, there will have been no discussion with the admiral about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, the -- there are three matters in issue. Cross-examination of the witness recalled in rebuttal pursuant to the leave we've given will be limited to matters that have a clear relevance to the two items that are the subject of the leave to call the evidence. That is the alleged briefing on the 5th of December and the alleged telephone conversation on the 6th of December with General Kadijevic. Now, that -- it may be that some matter a little before or a little after either of those events can be shown to have a very clear and direct relevance to one of those topics. If that is the case, the Chamber would be prepared to allow the cross-examination to extend to that. But a very careful and limited view will be taken of that. So it has got to be clearly and obviously directly relevant. This evidence is being led by way of rebuttal by leave of the Chamber only because of failures, which we spoke about when granting the leave, on the part of the Defence. In view of that, it is the Chamber's view that this recall of the witness should not be allowed to extend to the Defence putting to him the three further documents which have been mentioned by Mr. Petrovic. Were it not for the Defence's failure, which we've discussed earlier, there would simply not be this opportunity to call the admiral and put matters to him, and we think we should hold them to the narrow confines of that. With respect to the fourth document, the diary, as this was discovered by the Prosecution only a few days ago for the first time and is directly relevant for matters that were canvassed in the evidence, we would allow the diary to be put to the admiral if recalled. To that end and for that purpose, the Chamber will now adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we ready for the witness now, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We are, sir. And thank you. The Prosecution appreciates your permission the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My watch must be faulty today. I thought it was much longer than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We apologise. Thank you very much. For the record, the Prosecution calls in rebuttal Admiral Miodrag Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Admiral. Could you take the affirmation card and make a fresh affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. You have been recalled to deal briefly with a few matters, Admiral. I think that's probably been explained to you. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I'm going to ask you about a couple of areas, and I would like because of the time, we are on very limited time, to ask you for your answers to be focussed and concise. Admiral, you have testified briefly that on the 5th of December 1991, after the negotiations in Cavtat, you reported to General Strugar in Trebinje between 1500 and 1600 hours and returned to your command post in Kupari. What did you do in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: In Kupari, I informed my command about the fact that a cease-fire had been agreed, that a cease-fire would take place the next day at 1200 hours, that everything has practically been accepted and agreed to, but that the cease-fire would be signed on the 6th. I told the chief of staff to inform the units that the cease-fire should be observed, that no units should move, that no operations should take place, and that they should remain in their respective areas of deployment. Also, I ordered that a regular report be sent to the command of the 2nd Operational Group. Pursuant to the order of the 2nd Operational Group, we had to draft a combat order in relation to the following day, the 6th of December, and send it on to our subordinate commands. After that, I left for Kumbor. There was no briefing there. In Cavtat, when I signed the agreement, I called Zec and told him that there would be no briefing. Therefore, Zec knew about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was no briefing, Admiral, where are you referring to "there was no briefing"? In what location was there no briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The briefing at the forward command post in Kupari where briefings were normally held and where any action and operations were prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the manner in which you relayed or conveyed to your command about the fact that a cease-fire had been agreed? If it wasn't a briefing, what was the manner in which this was done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This was relayed through a combat order and by telephone, by dispatch and by telephone. Each unit commander received this order. The chief of staff had been informed as early as at 1500 hours that a cease-fire had been agreed. He called me on the phone at Cavtat, and he knew about this even before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at Kupari itself, in what manner did you actually make the notification of the fact of the proposed cease-fire or the cease-fire and the negotiations? How did you do that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Orally. To my command, orally. As for the commanders of subordinate units, I did it in writing and by telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the concept of a briefing, of a briefing, what was your practice with respect to briefings? When would you hold a briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Briefings would take place on an almost daily basis, but I did not attend those briefings. I was present whenever preparations were underway for an operation or if it was necessary to discuss a particular problem with the commanders. Therefore, whenever it was important, I chaired the briefing. This briefing at the same time would constitute some sort of preparation for an upcoming operation then. This was usually the case twice a week. If I wasn't the one who chaired the meeting, then it was the chief of staff. So in my absence, it was the chief of staff who chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you had -- when you were present at a briefing, who would normally be present if you were present?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The chief of staff was always there, chief of operations, as well as the assistant commander for ground forces. Specifically, Zec, Kozaric, and Colonel Gavrilo Kovacevic. As for the heads of the combat arms and branches, those whose presence was required, the chief of communications, artillery, anti-aircraft defence, whoever's presence was required. And it depended very much on the tasks that were being handed out, and the assistant commander for security would also be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it likely that a company commander would attend a briefing at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. Certainly not. A company commander would certainly not attend a briefing or a meeting where operations were being prepared. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would a battalion commander go?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: A battalion commander, yes, if it was an independent battalion. For example, the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade and the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade had to be there, had to be present. Because those were independent commanders and they were detached from their brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, for example, a battalion commander could not be present at a briefing or otherwise have representation, can a company commander as a designated substitute for a battalion commander attend such a briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. Only if the battalion commander loses his assistants. He had an assistant for political activities and an assistant for intelligence affairs. And some battalions also had an assistant for security. Therefore, if none of these assistants were around, which was hardly likely, then perhaps the commander himself could have appointed someone else. But this was never the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give an approximate time, approximate time, as to when you arrived in Kupari? Approximate time, what time of day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact time, but I think between 4.00 and 5.00. If you look at the agenda of the meeting, if you look at the when the cease-fire was signed and when we had lunch and when I eventually told General Strugar, I arrived in Kupari. I must say I was in a hurry, very much so, in fact, because we had a problem to deal with. A ship had been sunk, and the Pula sector had to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking to the 5th of December, the time you're just discussing, when you were at Kupari, who else was there? Who else was present, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that the chief of staff was there, Zec, Colonel Kovacevic was there, and Frigate Captain Kozaric. As for the others, I don't remember who they were. But there probably were other officers present, too, who worked at the operations centre or were involved with the communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, no, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an individual named Miroslav Jovanovic, the acting commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. He was not the commander of the 3rd Battalion. He only came as an indispensable stand-in, and he spent only two days in the unit, and I didn't have any chance of seeing him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him? Did you know Miroslav Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct what would have been perhaps the type of subject matter you said took place at a briefing when you were at Kupari on the 5th of December? You described earlier that actions would be the subject. Did you conduct a briefing, was there an action that would have required a briefing in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need for that. There was no need for that whatsoever. I only informed them that I would be in Kumbor, and everybody was aware what the subject matter would be. And the people in Kumbor would handle the problem of acquainting the units with the agreement and the writing of the reports, and that was the only thing I informed the command of. Where I will be and what I would be doing, I also told them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you also said that no, there was no need for a briefing. Why was there no need for a briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Because after the 13th of December -- sorry, 13th November, apart from minor provocations, we did not have any operations or actions in the area around Dubrovnik. And in the broader area of Croatia, the stabilisation of cease-fire and peace was already on the horizon, the arrival of new negotiators had been announced. It was expected that the level of negotiators would be raised to ministerial, and we were not expecting any new assignment involving a new operation or action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, Admiral, were records- records- kept of meetings -- any meetings or briefings, were records normally kept?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a log -- there was a log recording the briefings, including the date of the briefing, when the briefing was done, who made the reports, who chaired the briefing, and the subject --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information we received yesterday at 11.30 about what this witness would be testifying about is completely opposite to what the current testimony of this witness. So I would kindly ask that this part of his testimony be deleted from the record. And I can read out what our learned friends sent us last night on this subject, that the witness had just spoken to if there is any dispute. 3

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you'd just wait a moment, please, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The -- excuse me. It's possible that the way I framed the question to him is not as clearly framed as it was yesterday, but the assertion is correct that Mr. Petrovic has made about records. But if the Admiral is in a position perhaps to flush it out, there is a second part to it that I have not gotten to yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know what all that is saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Specifically, the portion in the proofing summary, if -- may I inform the Chamber of it, records were not kept of such meetings, but orders and reports may have been issued as a result of the meeting -- of the briefings. And that was part 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going to move on to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, would orders or reports or matters concerning orders or reports have been in some way resulting from briefings and might those orders or reports have found their way in some way recorded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is why -- that is what I wanted to clarify. I hadn't understood you. You were talking about briefings and meetings, and that is why I said that no records in writing were made. However, you have to make one distinction: In our military practice of the JNA, when you say "briefing," a record is kept without fail. However, you didn't ask me last night about briefings, the making of reports. You asked me about briefings as meetings. And in that sense, I meant that records were not kept. However, if it was a briefing where reports are made, of course, records were kept according to regulation that is prescribed. That is why I'm clarifying our discussion tonight. In the making of reports at a briefing, a log is kept of who was reporting on what subject and when. That is the kind of briefing that is recorded. However, when there is a meeting discussing preparation of an action or operation, there is no record of that because subsequently orders are issued, and then there is no need to write a record of the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the document we received last night, it reads: [In English] "... By his senior command staff and battalion commanders once or twice a week as required during periods of action. Records were not kept of such meetings, but orders and reports may have been issued as a result of the briefings." [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I think Ms. Somers and you are in agreement over what was exchanged, and the admiral has just explained how Ms. Somers asked a question which he understood one way and answered it. That's how it has arisen. But I take it you're not about to suggest there is a log that you are going to tender, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Admiral. Admiral, approximately how long were you at the forward command post at Kupari on the 5th of December discussing the cease-fire with your subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We didn't get an interpretation of that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake. The channel was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we'll have to have it again, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, approximately how long were you at the forward command post at Kupari on the 5th of December discussing the cease-fire with your subordinate commanders approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: As I said, around 30 minutes, maybe more or less. It could have been longer. It could have been shorter. But I would certainly be there for 30 minutes. I cannot tell you more precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, regarding the interpretation, the answer that is missing in the record and it can be checked in the audiotape. The answer given originally was 30 to 60 minutes. That's what the witness said first, and we can check that on the recording of today's hearing. That was the reason to my objection relating what the witness said. Second, Your Honours, in this document we received last night, it says that he was there between 20 minutes and half an hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The present evidence is approximately 30 minutes. It may be more, it may be less, I can't be sure. I think that's -- which is closer to that which you had notice of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Admiral, I'm going to ask you, did you on the 5th of December 1991, did you conduct either a briefing or a meeting, call it what you will, at the forward command post at Kupari where a plan to attack Srdj was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in any meeting or discussion on the 5th of December 1991 where Captain Vladimir Kovacevic of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd complained of the Croat provocations and proposed to carry out an attack on Srdj to counter the same?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, definitely not. I did not see Captain Kovacevic on that day, and I don't believe I saw him on the previous day either, on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, or the 6th of December 1991, did you at any time authorise the provision of fire support from the 130-millimetre cannons in Cilipi in support of an attack on Srdj to be carried out on 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I certainly did not. On the contrary, I ordered Captain Kozaric to convey to the chief of staff that no cannons may be used for support, I mean the cannons of the 9th sector. So quite the contrary. I warned them that that was out of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, I'm talking about on the 5th of December --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was talking about the 6th. On the 5th, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of any officer, commander, commanding officer or officer in the 9th VPS command promising Captain Vladimir Kovacevic of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade to provide the 130-millimetre cannon fire in support of the attack carried out on 6th December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And generally speaking, I want to add one thing, it was simply impossible because Captain Kovacevic knew perfectly well that he could not receive support without the approval of the commander. As a commander himself, he was very well aware of that. So that was out of the question. It would have been impossible for an officer from my command to promise the support from those guns to the commander of the 3rd Battalion. And I dare even say that it is impossible. The chief of staff would have been the person who could have allowed it or promised it, but on the condition that he informs me, and he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If such an order were to have been made in advance, let us say on the 5th, would it have to be in writing? In what form would that order take? I'm sorry, what form would that order take? Excuse my framing.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, it would have been in writing because those are guns of a large calibre, because there was no operation or action, because such guns are used only in emergencies and very rarely because their effective range is up to 24 kilometres. So without a written order, it would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Admiral, of any written order authorising the 130-millimetre cannon fire supporting the attack carried out on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not aware of that. I never had any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, did you ever participate in the planning of an attack on Srdj to be carried out on 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Vladimir Kovacevic of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd regularly attend meetings at the forward command post in Kupari, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He attended those meetings rather seldom. If I remember correctly, he attended only a few times. He always excused himself on account of the problems he allegedly had in his companies, and he went more frequently to Trebinje, to the command of the 2nd Operations Group than to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. Both the question and the answer go beyond the scope of what was indicated as the subject matter of today's examination. So I move that all of this answer Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond be deleted from the record. Not a word of it was indicated in the document distributed to us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm searching through what is there, Ms. Somers, to see if any part of it can be said to directly be within the scope of our leave. And I have difficulty seeing that it does. Do you have any submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that the subject matter is briefings, and very central to the issue was the presence of Captain Kovacevic. And if there's a particular briefing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And it's a particular briefing, and the question was and the evidence of the admiral whether the captain was there or not. You are going on to a general discussion of the subject matter, too wide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we have crept, we apologise. We'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Upheld, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment, Your Honour, pursuant to that ruling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that a Miroslav Jovanovic temporarily replaced the permanent commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, a Major Srboljub Zdravkovic who was on leave. If you recall, when did Major Zdravkovic go on leave and when did Jovanovic replace him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I think it could have been on the 4th of December. I'm not sure, however, exactly when it was. But Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic spent two days in the unit according to the inquiries I made in the course of the preparation of my case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this -- generally -- specifically to this time period, why did you allow Zdravkovic to take leave on the 5th of December? After all, he was a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate it if my learned friend would look at what the witness said on page 19, line 25, and take care when she is asking questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why at this time period did you allow a battalion commander to go on leave, to take leave?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Because the tactical situation was stable, no combat activities or operations were planned. There was no reason to expect any surprises, and there was no reason to refuse him leave because he had a family problem. Somebody in his family was ill, and I believe his leave was five days, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Miroslav Jovanovic, to the best of your knowledge, ever attend a meeting or briefing conducted by you at the forward command post in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I'm saying once again, he spent only two days in the unit, and he was not able to attend any meetings. He simply couldn't have attended any meetings which I participated in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 6th of December 1991 attack, why did you replace Miroslav Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I replaced him because he had given artillery support to the attack on Mount Srdj led by Captain Kovacevic, as requested by Captain Kovacevic, without anyone's approval. Without my approval specifically. I also found out how many shells had been fired, namely, how many shells had been fired from his weapons on targets in Dubrovnik town, which made me very angry, and that's why I replaced him without even giving him an opportunity to be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As Jovanovic was merely acting for the permanent battalion commander, in replacing him, what did you have in mind? Was it in terms of a formal disciplinary measure, or did you have him removed from his temporary position, that temporary position being the acting battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely how it was. I removed him practically from the position of battalion commander; that is, acting battalion commander. I returned him to his original unit because he was unable to perform the duty he had come to perform. He was irresponsible, and he acted irresponsibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the attack on the 6th of December, did you personally meet Miroslav Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Miroslav Jovanovic sought out a meeting with you on the 6th of December or after the 6th of December to inquire from you as to why he had been replaced?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I never heard anything of the kind. I don't believe it's true. I don't believe that he would have dared to appear before me, seeing that I had replaced him by telephone. I don't believe he was brave enough to come and see me and look for an explanation. I don't think that is likely, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miroslav Jovanovic testified before this Chamber that he was present at a briefing at the forward command post in Kupari on the 5th of December 1991 where he claimed you chaired a meeting at which the attack on Srdj the following day, that is, the 6th of December, was discussed. Did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Definitely not. I concluded a total cease-fire. Why would I be going to prepare an attack on Srdj the next thing? That's absolutely absurd. If I had done that, Strugar would have been informed within an hour, and so would have General Kadijevic, I think. Every regular soldier understands that. If I were preparing within my command an attack against the feature after having concluded a cease-fire with Mr. Rudolf two hours earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask, please, that Admiral Jokic be shown Exhibit D96.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to an explicit question put by the Defence yesterday as to whether any exhibits would be used and whether any documents would be shown, the answer was no. Also, also, in the document that was submitted to us about this, there is no mention of that whatsoever, that any document would be discussed or that any document would be shown to this witness. So could this line of questioning, the one espoused by my colleague just now, could it please be abandoned all altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this relates directly to the allegations about the use of 130 millimetres. The reference that is sought is on page 68 at 8.36, and it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're not dealing with the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: About the use of the document. It is correct, Your Honours, that it is not specifically stated, but we had not at the time of the -- excuse me one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm reminded that the delegation of responsibilities yesterday when I spoke with the Trial Chamber or with counsel was not necessarily conveyed to my colleagues who were at the Detention Centre, and they did not know to put the document to the admiral. And at that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the topic of this document the use of 130-millimetre cannon?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is a specific entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the document is in evidence. You can refer to it in your submissions. How does this directly arise from the leave that has been granted?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This relates to the alleged promise of the use of the weaponry. I can certainly move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you'd better. I've got to say, in my understanding, I am surprised how much you are making of these two issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We will move on. Thank you for that. Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about the 6th of December, Admiral. On the 6th of December 1991, except for your meeting with General Kadijevic in Belgrade, did you have a telephone conversation with General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I was informed that General Kadijevic and General Adzic had telephoned me, and that this message had come to the desk in the operations room. However, I did not conduct a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if General Kadijevic attempted to telephone you on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I heard that he had tried, yes. Both General Kadijevic and General Adzic and Admiral Kandic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Kumbor the main switchboard from which the telephone links from Belgrade could be established to Kupari or Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. The communications centre in Kumbor could establish communications for the commander wherever he was. However, the centre for communications in Kupari, although it was mobile, could establish for the commander any communication that was necessary. Also, the communications centre in Trebinje, General Strugar's centre, it was absolutely capable in the same way of establishing communications for the commander in order to be able to carry out his command. Technically, that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If General Kadijevic wanted you to contact him, would he call -- is it your understanding that your forward command post in Kupari would be called or the peacetime command in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly now who they would call first. However, had General Kadijevic wanted to, he would have first called his next person down the chain of command, and that was General Strugar. And only then he would call me. Then he, and his people who did that for him, first established where which person was. They knew that I was in Kupari from where the command was taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a direct telephone link from Belgrade to Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a regular line or was it a secure line?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: It was a safe, radio relay line protected from possible eavesdropping, yes. Yes. It was channelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an individual named Petre Handzijev?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he responsible for staffing the switchboard at the Kumbor operations centre during the time period --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he responsible for staffing the switchboard at the Kumbor operations centre?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. He was one of the officers who were operations duty officers at the operations centre in Kumbor. Communications were not his sector. He's a naval officer. He's not a communications officer, a signals officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was a record kept of communications including telephone calls from officials at the level of the federal secretary of defence, General Kadijevic, to the various command posts?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: According to regulations, every communications centre has its own logbook, the so-called station logbook. And in the operations centre, all communications that were established have to be recorded. That is to say, those aimed -- those that were coming in and those that were going out of the centre. As far as the federal secretary is concerned, it is certainly that that link could not have been missed. If anything could not have been missed, it's that kind of link, I mean to have a record that such a telephone communication was established, such a communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Very briefly, where were such records kept, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: At the operations centre, at the operations centre room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, what was the role of the communications officer? Again, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He was not a communications officer in the sense of a communications officer, a signals officer, as the general term goes. I'm talking about a signalsman who is on duty at the operations centre. He is on duty at the operations centre. He establishes communication for those for whom communication is required. So this is a duty officer at the communications centre, at the operations centre. He knows what the technical problems are relating to all the equipment, and he's responsible for radio relay communications, radio communications, teleprinter, encrypted teleprinter communications, all types of equipment both technically and from the point of view of operations. And also he is the duty officer for his particular shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, Admiral, returning to Petre Handzijev, did you have personal dealings with Petre Handzijev?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, when necessary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your experience as to his abilities as an officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I've known him for many years, more than ten years, 10 or 12 years. He was an officer who was below average. His grades were usually around 3. He was a very poor speaker. He could not express himself. His professional abilities were the poorest of all. And that is why his advancement was so slow, his assessments were very low.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say his -- I think you used the term "his grades were usually around 3." What is the scale? 3 out of...?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The scales were from poor, that is to say, a negative grade, and then there was the grade "good," the grade "exceeds performance criteria," and the ultimate one as a rule exceeds performance criteria. His was the grade that is called good, so that it would not be a negative, nonpassing grade. Also, he had many failings. He did not complete the higher military academy. He did not carry out specialist training. He did not complete specialist training, everything that an officer is supposed to go Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond through in order to be promoted either on a fast track or on a regular pace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, were you involved in the evaluation of the performance of Petre Handzijev?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, in this stage, I was not, I mean while I was commander there. It was not for me to do that. But ten years before that, I was chief of operations, and then I followed that. And also later on, I was chief of staff, and then I followed this in detail. And now, in this stage that we are discussing now, I could not follow that because his superior was Kozaric, Frigate Captain Kozaric, and his second commander in line was Zec. But I think the situation did not change too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have to sign off or put an endorsement in the -- as you were in the chain of command on his evaluations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed official evaluations for him in the last instance, yes. So I was aware of it. I was aware of the actual assessment made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how often Captain Kozaric graded or evaluated Mr. Handzijev, and if you know of an individual named Drljan as well, how often were they evaluated, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, there are regulations on official evaluation. As far as I can remember, official evaluation is carried out every fourth year, if that is what was in force all the time. In my day, it was. If somebody received a poor assessment, then he had to be reassessed every year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would your evaluations or your endorsement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the information that we received is not four years or one year. It says here two years. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, is there a fixed period, if you recall, for how often an evaluation must take place?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying as far as I can remember, and that is what I stated previously, I was not sure whether it's two or four years. But having given it some thought, I think it was four years. Of course, I can't be sure of that. But if the assessment was not good, if it was negative, then the person had to be reassessed every year to check whether it was possible to give the person a positive evaluation after all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "having given it some thought," are you suggesting that between yesterday and now you have given it additional thought?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would your evaluations have affected his career? When I say "your evaluations," ones that were signed off ultimately by you or at some point by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am sorry for taking this precious time, but there is no mention of this in the document that I have here before me, not a single word.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is a natural by-product of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is going almost beyond the limits of what might be contemplated by the leave, if I might say, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is just going on far unnecessarily long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have two more questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, Petre Handzijev testified that he forwarded a telephone call from General Kadijevic to you on the 6th of December 1991. He testified that he heard part of the alleged conversations and said that General Kadijevic asked you what was going on, and that you responded in a confused manner, that you were carrying out some tactical movements. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This is complete nonsense, that I was carrying out some tactical movements? No way, absolutely not. There is nothing I have to say to that. I could not have said any such thing. That is one matter. Secondly, I cannot even find the right word. But I am deeply suspicious of the possibility of him eavesdropping on that kind of conversation, that he would have dared listen to a conversation between his commander and the federal secretary of defence. In that operations room, there were at least five or six persons who are present and who would have to hear all of that. And thirdly, I'm not sure that technically Handzijev was capable of doing that, to eavesdrop on that conversation, and without that being noticed because he is not a signalsman. He is a naval officer who came from a ship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Final question: Was Handzijev aware of your views as to capabilities as an officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Well, every officer has to know, especially if he is close to the commander, what the commander thinks of him and of his promotion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the questions will be put my colleague, Mr. Rodic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jokic, could you please tell me when you concluded the negotiations in Cavtat on the 5th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: After 14 years, I cannot know exactly what time it was. But I think it could have been around 2.00. Around 1400 hours. Between 13 and 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be a bit more precise?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I cannot. I think it was around that time. It could not have been before 1300 hours, and I don't think it was after 1400 hours. So it's within that interval. And you will appreciate that 14 years later without a single document to that effect, I simply cannot know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the time between 13 and 1400 hours. That is when the negotiations in Cavtat ended, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot be very accurate, but I'm telling you what I remember to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, what did you do after you finished the negotiations in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: What did I do? We had a luncheon, this delegation with the negotiators, that is to say, the negotiators and the representatives of the European Community. We had a joint luncheon that went on for about an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The negotiators, the representatives of the European Community, do you remember members of the monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ministers from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that luncheon went on for about an hour, do you remember then when you left Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps around 3.00, around 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: To Trebinje to report to the commander of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how you travelled to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: In a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time do you need approximately to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: About 20 minutes, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you stayed in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Not long, I think. As far as I can remember, I reported on how the negotiations went, that basically all their requirements were met, or rather, all the items of the agreement, and the final question --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. But we've already heard that. We've already heard that answer from you. I'm just interested in the time so that we could move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Oh, the time. Up to half an hour. Not more than that, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, after this half hour in Trebinje, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: To the command post in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time do you need from Trebinje to Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: 20 minutes, 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The time you mentioned in your answer in response to my learned friend's question, the time that you spent in Kupari, about half an hour, do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. That is my present-day recollection, but how can I know for sure after 14 years?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you're answering my questions, you don't remember. But when you're answering the Prosecutor's questions, you do remember.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I said the same thing. I said between half an hour and an hour. I said I was not sure. But since I was in a hurry and there was no briefing or debriefing, there was no preparation for action, there was no need to spend more than half an hour there. That is the only logical answer the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why were you in a hurry to leave Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Because we had a problem of evacuating the Pula sector. There was a standstill in the evacuation by boats, and there was an incident in the town of Pula. Fire was opened. There were some threats and so on. At the same time, there was the problem of the sinking of one of our ships which was sunk in the waters around Vis. And I knew some of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me briefly, in relation to what you said to us just now, did you take any action or measures in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. I was with the logistics assistant, and certainly with other officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you were engaged during the course of that day in these activities related to the sinking of the ship and the incidents in Pula?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know how long. But I certainly didn't go to bed between -- before 10.00 or 11.00 that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector, did you ever spent the night at the forward command post in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what "very often" would mean in terms of one week approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, during the course of a week, perhaps I would be at home in the apartment once; two or three times in Kumbor; and the same amount of time in Kupari. Perhaps I spent more time in Kumbor than in Kupari. That's possible. I allow for that possibility, that I spent more nights in Kumbor than in Kupari when there was a lull --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, all right. Tell me, please, on the 5th of December when you finished the negotiations, did Zec call you before lunch with the negotiators or after the lunch with the negotiators?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I think it was before lunch. But I cannot be sure of that. I'm not sure of that. Now, whether Sofronije Jeremic called Kupari and then spoke to him, I know that Jeremic gave me the telephone, but I don't know when that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly what it was that you told Battleship Captain Zec exactly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, I told him the talks had been concluded, that there was an agreement that had been reached which was consistent with their own ideas, that there was to be a cease-fire and that there were no orders for our units to move. I said that after lunch I'd be going to Trebinje first, and then I'd be in Kupari and there would be no briefing. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to Zec about the total cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell him in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I told him formally speaking, this has not yet been signed on account of the checks to be carried out in relation to the ships. But fire mustn't be opened as of 12.00. That's what I told him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us specify, please: Did you tell Zec on the 5th of December once the negotiations had been concluded that there was to be a total cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't have told him that a total cease-fire would take place. I said that fire mustn't be opened. A formal total cease-fire had not been ordered, and it wasn't for me to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him anything about a total cease-fire, a total peace, when this was supposed to take place or when this was expected to take place or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I told him that formally speaking, the next day at 1100 hours we would be signing the agreement. And that's why 1200 hours was the time that was recorded, but that none of the commanders were to open fire and all of the commanders were to be informed about this. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you did tell him not to hold a briefing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I told him that I wouldn't be holding a briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Wasn't he the one who was to be holding a briefing that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say whether any of the commanders were there with him. There is no way for me to know that. If he had planned to hold a briefing, probably he would have told me, or he would have told me about a briefing he held or of some preparations perhaps. But I knew of no such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zec did, in fact, hold a briefing on that day or not? Do you know that? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's quite sufficient. You said that on that day you did not hold any briefing with your subordinate commanders. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you issue Zec any instructions during that telephone call as to what he should do with regard to the -- to information that you had given him about the negotiations in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, no fire was to be opened. The units were not to move anywhere from their areas of deployment. The commanders were not to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond wait for me because there would be no briefing, and I was on my way to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say anything about Zec being supposed to inform the subordinate units in the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How exactly was he supposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He was to inform all the commanders that they mustn't open fire, that an agreement, a peace agreement, had been signed and there would be a combat order in due course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, don't take up any more of my time. Just answer my questions briefly, please. How exactly was Milan Zec supposed to inform the subordinate commanders, by telephone, in writing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Both. By telephone and in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I know because he told me, and all the commanders knew. They knew full well, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. I'll have to reask a question because your answer was not recorded in the transcript. So question, did Zec inform the subordinate commanders by telephone or by a written order that a peace agreement and cease-fire had been agreed upon and that no operations were to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He informed me, and I'm sure the commanders knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember the time, what time it was by the time you arrived in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I know it was dark, and according to the time indication that you have used, it may have been between 1600 hours and 1700 hours. Possibly 1630 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, and if you could give me the names of the people who were at that lunch in Cavtat with you on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: On our side, in addition to myself, frigate Captain Jeremic was present and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't. I think the first name was Zeljko, but I don't know his last name. He was from Herceg Novi, a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I please remind you, was it Zeljko Uljarevic or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Herceg Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, what about the -- what about your opposite number?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Three ministers were there and a representative of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about after lunch? As a good host, did you see them off?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember. Yes, I did. I really can't remember specifically where we had lunch, but the negotiations had taken place at a small hotel on the seaside promenade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they reach Cavtat, by which means of transport?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: By ship. They came by ship. It was a small sailing boat that was used for touristic purposes. The name was "ARGOS," the name of the boat, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When they arrived in Cavtat, did you welcome them there as they arrived by ship, by boat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw them off the same way, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite certain. I think I held the rope for the sailor because the sailor ran out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P162.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, on the 5th of December -- can you please leave that diary for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm listening to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, when was the meeting supposed to take place? When was it supposed to begin, the meeting with the negotiators?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I think at 1100 hours, but I can't be sure. I can't remember specifically. There was supposed to be a meeting at 1100 hours the next day and the signing of the agreement. And on that day, it had been delayed, but I can't think for when exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was certainly in the morning, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at around noon, at around 1200 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document you have before you is a radio log of the Dubrovnik naval authorities, maritime authorities. Can you please look at that document. A recording at 8.15 hours, "'ARGOS' leaving port with representatives of the European Community and setting sail for Cavtat." Did you find that entry at 15 past 8.00?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the boat with the representatives of the European Community who left for Cavtat to attend negotiations with you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 7. Look at the entry at 12.16 hours, "'ARGOS' leaving Cavtat. Should be in the Old Town port in half an hour." And the next entry at 12.48 hours: "'ARGOS' reaching the Old Town port." As you were the person who saw them off, does that mean, Mr. Jokic, that they had reached the Old Town port as soon as 12.48 hours, the negotiators?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The time that I remember is quite different, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll no longer be requiring that document. You can put it away for the time being. You can leave it right there. Can we show the Witness P61 now, tab 29. Do you perhaps remember Mr. Per Hvalkof who was a member of the monitoring mission of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a man named that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the diary that Mr. Hvalkof kept on behalf of the monitoring mission. The mark is: "Meeting between Minister Rudolf and Admiral Jokic in Cavtat, 1000 hours to 1300 hours 5th of December 1991." Did the European monitors wait until Mr. Rudolf and you, Admiral, concluded your meeting? Did they attend the talks you had with the minister or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't attend. It was my proposal that they should not be present in order to make -- in order to expedite the meeting, and that's why we did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 3, paragraph 3, "Minister Rudolf said that the following subjects had been discussed: (A), unconditional cease-fire between Dubrovnik and Ploce to take effect 24 hours after the signing of the agreement." Is that what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: That's not what the agreement said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the 6th of December? Do you remember when the talks were to be continued?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: At 1100 hours, I believe. Possibly at 1000 hours. It must have been either 10.00 or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, in the interview that you gave the investigators of the Tribunal in July 2002, why did you state that you had concluded business in Cavtat by lunchtime and that you had sent a report to the commander of the 2nd OG and issued orders to chief of staff Zec in relation to the cease-fire and then that you had left Cavtat for Kumbor? Once that was successfully concluded, you believed that there was no need for you to meet with your command, which we see on page 175 of the English version. The ERN number is 03084753.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that very well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. This is between General Strugar and Admiral Zec. That is not a focal part of the rebuttal direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was very much part of the evidence that you took us through. Carry on, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can provide an explanation if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 176 -- my apologies, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I can explain why I said at the time that I was headed for Kumbor from Cavtat and not to Trebinje or to Kupari. I have already explained in a different interview. It should be in the files. But if you want, I can repeat. In July 2002, I couldn't remember whether I had informed the command of the 2nd Operational Group by telephone or in person. There were thousands of questions being asked, and I hadn't talked to anyone, not to Zec, not to Kozaric, not to my officers, not to Sofronije Jeremic and so on and so forth. However, after that interview in July, I talked to a lot of different officers, and I established that the route I took was exactly as I told you today. The times may differ, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. In your answer, what has not been recorded is about you not being able to remember back at the time whether you had informed your command and the command of the 2nd Operational Group. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, do I take it that you'll be a little while yet? We had better break for the tapes and the interpreters. We'll resume at just after 5 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate to both counsel, the admiral has a Pre-Trial Conference this afternoon. The Judge conducting that has agreed to delay the start of it. That puts us under time constraints. And therefore, we must ask you to finish at the very latest by 10 minutes to, Mr. Rodic. And that will give Prosecution five minutes' re-examination. Thank you. And that will then give the admiral time to collect his thoughts before he needs to go to the pre-trial, which will start at 3.30, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, in your interview of July 2000 given to the investigators, on page 176 of the English version, in response to the question of the investigator whether after lunch you had a meeting with the chief of staff or only talk to him, what -- in fact, how did you say it to him? Your answer was: "I believe I phoned him from the command in Cavtat because the situation was stable, the cease-fire had been concluded, we had no particular commitments which would force me to issue any orders to the commanders." Question: "Where did you call him on the phone? Where was he?" Answer: "He was for sure in Kupari at the forward command post." Is that what you stated, Mr. Jokic, in July 2000 -- 2002?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now you are saying something different.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't think I'm saying anything different. What I said then was I thought that's what I did. The question was, "did I," and I said, "I thought." However, after talking to the officers in Kupari and after talking to the command, I established that after all, I did go to inform them, and I informed General Strugar at the command as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. On page 176 of the interview given in July 2002, the question of the investigator reads: "And then you went to Kumbor following Zec?" Correction, "with Zec." "A. No, I went alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After calling very much from Kupari, you called Cavtat. Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: To Kumbor." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But after that July interview, there were another two interviews dealing with the same subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 177, I quote the question of the investigator: "Q. So that was the situation of the 5th of December. You had signed the order. You went to Kumbor. And you didn't meet any more with any officers of the JNA, with no one from the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes." Is that what you stated, Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, if that is what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 204 of the interview of July 2002, the question of the investigate reads: "In your opinion on that morning, was Zec executing the orders given by you?" The subject was the 6th of December 1991. Your answer was: "I think basically yes, but I was surprised at how slow it was moving on, the withdrawal of the units. That was making me very angry and I was very concerned. And when Kozaric told me once that there were a lot of casualties because of that artillery of theirs, I said he has his own artillery and let him neutralise those sources of fire." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: As to the first part, yes. But as far as the artillery is concerned, I don't believe I said it in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then tell me in what context it was, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
